title: Precessional world-age chronology
statement: Wheel of Heaven organizes long-range history as a Great Year of twelve equal world ages of 2,160 years each, an idealization of the astronomical precession cycle, anchored by project convention so that the Age of Aquarius spans 1950-4110 CE and the cycle opens with the Age of Capricorn about 21,810 BCE.

includes: The idealized Great Year model of twelve equal 2,160-year ages totaling 25,920 years
The project anchor convention fixing the Age of Aquarius at 1950-4110 CE and the cycle opening at circa 21,810 BCE
The stated relation of the model to observed axial precession: idealization, not measurement
excludes: Placement of specific events, figures, or interventions within ages
The thesis that ancient cultures possessed or encoded precessional knowledge
The canonical calendar's year-one as anything other than a source report

source_references.locator: Whole-work thesis that world mythology encodes precessional knowledge; exact passages not yet inspected
Journal for the History of Astronomy 3 (1972), pp. 206-211
Whole-work Aquarian periodization antedating the 1973 canonical report
Treatment of Hipparchus and the discovery of precession; exact pages not yet inspected
Modern precession theory and constants; exact chapter not yet inspected

alternatives.statement: Precession was discovered by Hipparchus in the second century BCE, and claimed mythological encodings of earlier precessional knowledge are modern retrojection.
Astronomically defined ages would be unequal and boundary-convention-dependent; the equal-twelve division is an astrological convention without observational content.
No astronomically privileged anchor year exists; competing systems place the Aquarian onset centuries apart, so any anchor is stipulated rather than discovered.
The recurring numbers 72, 2,160, and 25,920 derive from Babylonian sexagesimal arithmetic and later astrological systematization rather than from preserved precessional science.

revision_triggers: The corpus changes its anchor year or age spans.
A reproducible review materially changes the assessment of pre-Hipparchan precessional knowledge.
A public derivative asserts boundary years as astronomical facts rather than framework conventions.
Event-placement claims require their own versioned records.
The five-layer decomposition proves too compound for review and the layers need independently versioned claims.
